maps.area: EdgeQuake Rust HTTP API — router construction + auth middleware wiring (packages/edgequake/crates/edgequake-api)
maps.summary: The HTTP API is an axum Router built in two steps: routes.rs::create_router() declares every route and binds AppState, then server.rs::build_router() wraps it in a fixed stack of tower/axum layers. The ONLY auth layer attached to the router is api_key_auth (wired in commit ff03128). It is always layered on, but it is a runtime no-op unless EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY is set in the environment — AuthConfig::default() has enabled=false, and the middleware returns next.run() immediately when disabled. So by default NO authentication runs on any route; the entire API is open. There is no JWT auth layer/middleware on the router at all: JWT is only verified inside one handler (/api/v1/auth/me) by manually parsing the Bearer header and calling jwt_service.verify_token; every other endpoint (documents, query, chat, graph, tenants, etc.) performs zero auth. A tenant_rate_limit middleware and TenantContext extractor exist but rate limiting is never wired into any router, and TenantContext is an Infallible header-reader (no rejection), used only as soft multi-tenant context.

files.role: Builds the axum app (build_router): constructs AuthConfig from EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY env, attaches the api_key_auth layer + logging/CORS/compression/Swagger, runs the server
create_router(): declares all routes (health, /api ollama, /api/v1/*) and binds AppState; no auth attached here
Defines api_key_auth middleware + AuthConfig/AuthState, tenant_rate_limit (unwired), request_logging, request_id, and the TenantContext extractor
Issues JWTs (login/refresh) and is the ONLY place a JWT is verified — inside get_me handler, not a layer
AppState holds jwt_service (Arc<JwtService>) and auth_config; JWT service is available to handlers but not enforced by any middleware
Re-exports tenant_rate_limit/AuthState/RateLimitState (export only — tenant_rate_limit is never used)

findings.fact: The router is created in routes.rs::create_router() which declares all routes (health/ready/live/metrics, /ws/*, nested /api ollama routes, nested /api/v1 routes) and binds state with .with_state(state). No auth/middleware is attached at this layer.
findings.evidence: routes.rs:93-113 `pub fn create_router(state: AppState) -> Router { Router::new().route("/health"...).nest("/api", ollama_api_routes()).nest("/api/v1", api_v1_routes()).with_state(state) }`

findings.fact: server.rs::build_router() is where every middleware/layer is attached. The api_key_auth layer is the only auth layer; it is added directly onto create_router() via from_fn_with_state.
findings.evidence: server.rs:108-109 `let mut app = create_router(self.state.clone()).layer(middleware::from_fn_with_state(auth_state, api_key_auth));`

findings.fact: Default (always-on) layers, in addition to api_key_auth: DefaultBodyLimit(100MB), request_logging (from_fn), request_id (from_fn), TraceLayer. CORS, Compression, and Swagger UI are gated by ServerConfig flags which all default to true.
findings.evidence: server.rs:112-137 (.layer DefaultBodyLimit / request_logging / request_id / TraceLayer; if enable_cors -> CorsLayer Any/Any/Any; if enable_compression -> CompressionLayer; if enable_swagger -> .merge(SwaggerUi)). Defaults: server.rs:65-67 `enable_cors: true, enable_compression: true, enable_swagger: true`

findings.fact: api_key_auth is OPT-IN: AuthConfig is only enabled when EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY env var is set and non-empty; otherwise AuthConfig::default() is used with enabled=false. So the auth layer is present on every build but disabled by default.
findings.evidence: server.rs:96-106 `match std::env::var("EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY") { Ok(key) if !key.trim().is_empty() => AuthConfig::with_api_keys(...), _ => AuthConfig::default() }`; middleware.rs:103-105 default `enabled: false`

findings.fact: When EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY is unset/empty (the default), api_key_auth short-circuits to next.run() for ALL requests — no key required, no rejection. The entire HTTP API is therefore unauthenticated by default.
findings.evidence: middleware.rs:173-176 `// Skip auth if disabled\n if !config.enabled { return next.run(request).await; }`

findings.fact: There is NO JWT auth layer or JWT-validating middleware attached to the router. The only auth-related layer is api_key_auth. JWT verification happens solely inside the get_me handler, which manually parses the Authorization Bearer header and calls jwt_service.verify_token — not via a router layer or extractor.
findings.evidence: server.rs:36 imports only `api_key_auth, request_id, request_logging`; session.rs:257-267 (get_me) `let token = auth_header.strip_prefix("Bearer ")...; let claims = state.jwt_service.verify_token(token)...`

findings.fact: jwt_service exists in AppState and is wired into login/refresh (token issuance), but verify_token is called in only one place (the /auth/me handler). No other handler verifies a JWT, so all business endpoints (documents, query, chat, graph, tenants, costs, etc.) enforce no per-user/JWT auth.
findings.evidence: state/mod.rs:174-175 `pub jwt_service: Arc<edgequake_auth::JwtService>`; grep shows verify_token only at session.rs:266 across all of handlers/

findings.fact: When api_key_auth IS enabled, public (unauthenticated) paths are only /health, /ready, /live, /swagger-ui, /api-docs (matched by prefix via starts_with). Everything else requires the key — including /metrics, /ws/* websockets, the Ollama /api/* routes, and ALL /api/v1/* routes including /api/v1/auth/login.
findings.evidence: middleware.rs:107-113 public_paths list; middleware.rs:129-131 `is_public_path` uses `path.starts_with(p)`; routes.rs:99-102 (/metrics and /ws/* are NOT in public_paths); routes.rs:132 (/auth/login is under /api/v1 and not public)

findings.fact: api_key_auth accepts the key via `Authorization: Bearer <key>` OR `X-API-Key: <key>`, validated by plain string equality against the configured key list (no hashing/constant-time compare).
findings.evidence: middleware.rs:218-236 extract_api_key (Bearer then x-api-key); middleware.rs:134-136 `validate_api_key` uses `self.api_keys.iter().any(|k| k == key)`

findings.fact: Swagger UI is attached via .merge() AFTER all .layer() calls, so /swagger-ui and /api-docs routes sit outside the api_key_auth layer entirely (in addition to being whitelisted as public). They are always reachable when enable_swagger is true.
findings.evidence: server.rs:133-137 `app = app.merge(SwaggerUi::new("/swagger-ui").url("/api-docs/openapi.json", ApiDoc::openapi()))` placed after the .layer chain

findings.fact: A tenant_rate_limit middleware and RateLimitState exist and are publicly re-exported, but they are NEVER attached to any router and RateLimitState is never constructed in the server path. Rate limiting does not run.
findings.evidence: middleware.rs:287-355 tenant_rate_limit defined; lib.rs:119 re-exports it; grep for tenant_rate_limit/RateLimitState finds zero usages outside middleware.rs definition + lib.rs export (not in server.rs/routes.rs)

findings.fact: TenantContext is an axum FromRequestParts extractor with Rejection = Infallible — it never fails a request. It only reads X-Tenant-ID / X-Workspace-ID / X-User-ID headers and is used as soft multi-tenant context in ~43 handler files; it performs no authentication or authorization.
findings.evidence: middleware.rs:442 `type Rejection = std::convert::Infallible;` and middleware.rs:444-449 always `Ok(TenantContext::from_headers(...))`; used in 43 handler files (grep TenantContext under handlers/)

findings.fact: Layer execution order (inbound) is, from outermost to innermost: Compression -> CORS -> TraceLayer -> request_id -> request_logging -> DefaultBodyLimit -> api_key_auth -> route handler. api_key_auth was added first so it is innermost (runs just before the handler), but still covers every route in create_router().
findings.evidence: server.rs:108-129 layer add order (axum applies last-added layer as outermost); api_key_auth added at server.rs:109, compression last at server.rs:129

findings.fact: Commit ff03128 ('feat(security): wire opt-in API-key auth into the EdgeQuake router (P2)') is what attached api_key_auth; before it the middleware existed but was never wired, so the HTTP API enforced nothing. The commit touched only server.rs (+ a progress doc) and notes 'cargo check passes. Not runtime-tested.'
findings.evidence: `git show --stat ff03128`: message 'EdgeQuake ships a complete api_key_auth middleware that was never attached to the router...'; changed files server.rs (+27/-3) and Planning DEV/SECURITY-FIXES-PROGRESS.md

open_questions: The web app (apps/web lib/edgequake/client.ts) and MCP server reportedly forward EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY, but the dashboard sends a per-user JWT instead — if EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY is ever enabled, dashboard calls will 401 since there is no JWT auth path in the router. Is EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY actually set in any deployment env today? (Not verified here.)

The route doc comment in routes.rs:71-82 claims 'Most endpoints require authentication via Bearer JWT / X-API-Key' and that tenant context is extracted from JWT claims — this is aspirational/inaccurate vs the implemented router, which enforces neither by default. Worth confirming whether any reverse-proxy / network layer (Docker-internal-only port) is the real access control.
tenant_rate_limit is dead code in the HTTP server; confirm whether any other binary/crate mounts it or if it should be removed.

maps.area: EdgeQuake Rust auth primitives: JWT validation, API-key validation, and secret sourcing
maps.summary: EdgeQuake has a real JWT auth crate (edgequake-auth) with a JwtService (HS256), Argon2 password hashing, RBAC, and Axum extractors — but the secret it signs/verifies with is always the hardcoded default. AuthConfig::default() hardcodes jwt_secret = "change-me-in-production-256-bit-secret-key" (config.rs:51), and AuthConfig::from_env() (which reads JWT_SECRET) is never called in production — every AppState constructor builds JwtService from AuthConfig::default() (postgres.rs:293, memory.rs:46/182/272). The JWT Claims struct carries sub/role/iat/exp/nbf/jti plus optional iss/aud/tenant_id/workspace_id/metadata, but login only calls generate_token(), so tenant_id/workspace_id are never populated. JWTs are only used directly in the auth/session handlers (login/refresh/get_me); the real AuthUser/AuthState/RequireAdmin extractors are never wired into the router, so the validated identity is NOT propagated to data handlers. Downstream handlers instead read identity from unauthenticated, fully client-spoofable X-Tenant-ID/X-Workspace-ID/X-User-ID headers (TenantContext, used in 43 handler files). The only request-time API-key check is a non-constant-time String == comparison against an env-supplied key, disabled by default; DB-backed API keys are created/hashed but never validated on incoming requests.

Role enum (fail-open to User), User, ApiKey/ApiKeyAuth scope helpers, token request/response types

In-memory AppState factories; lines 46/182/272 also use AuthConfig::default() for JwtService
Separate api_key_auth middleware with its own AuthConfig; validate_api_key uses non-constant-time String ==; TenantContext extractor reads unauthenticated X-Tenant/Workspace/User-ID headers
build_router(): only middleware wired is api_key_auth, gated on EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY env (disabled by default); real edgequake-auth extractors never added
login/refresh/logout/get_me: only place JwtService is used at request time; login generates tokens without tenant/workspace claims
create/list/revoke API keys: hashes key with Argon2 to KV but hardcodes user_id='demo-user'; no incoming-request validation of stored keys exists
Core Config + from_env() (no JWT/auth fields at all; only DB/LLM/API host/port); ApiConfig.auth_enabled defaults false, api_keys empty

findings.evidence: edgequake-auth/src/config.rs:51  jwt_secret: "change-me-in-production-256-bit-secret-key".to_string(),

findings.fact: Every AppState constructor wires the JWT service from AuthConfig::default(), so the hardcoded secret is always used regardless of JWT_SECRET in the environment.
findings.evidence: state/postgres.rs:293-294  let auth_config = AuthConfig::default(); let jwt_service = Arc::new(JwtService::new(auth_config.clone())); (same pattern at state/memory.rs:46-47, 182-183, 272-273)

Validation enables exp and nbf checks with 30s leeway; algorithm is HS256 (Validation::default()), and aud/iss are NOT validated.
findings.evidence: edgequake-auth/src/jwt.rs:159-168  EncodingKey::from_secret(config.jwt_secret.as_bytes()); DecodingKey::from_secret(config.jwt_secret.as_bytes()); validation.validate_exp=true; validate_nbf=true; leeway=30

findings.evidence: edgequake-auth/src/jwt.rs:33-73 (sub:35, role:39, iat:43, exp:46, nbf:49, jti:52, iss:56, aud:60, tenant_id:64, workspace_id:68, metadata:72)

findings.fact: Login issues tokens via generate_token(user_uuid, role) which builds Claims::new() — tenant_id and workspace_id are left None. So multi-tenancy claims are never populated into real tokens despite existing in the struct.
findings.evidence: handlers/auth/session.rs:81-87 generate_token(user_uuid, user.role); jwt.rs:79-90 Claims::new sets tenant_id:None, workspace_id:None

findings.fact: A validated JWT produces AuthUser { user_id: Uuid, role: Role, claims } with tenant_id()/workspace_id() accessors — but this identity is only constructed by the AuthUser/AuthState extractors, which are NEVER wired into the API router. Grep for AuthUser/RequireAdmin/RequireUser/CombinedAuth/FromRef in handlers and router returns no matches; no edgequake_auth::AuthState is ever constructed in the api crate.
findings.evidence: extractors.rs:33-56 extract_user builds AuthUser; grep AuthUser|RequireAdmin|RequireUser|CombinedAuth in crates/edgequake-api/src/handlers → no matches; grep extractors::AuthState / AuthState::new(jwt...) in api → none

findings.fact: Downstream identity is taken from unauthenticated, client-supplied headers X-Tenant-ID / X-Workspace-ID / X-User-ID via TenantContext, with no signature/verification. TenantContext is consumed in 43 handler files (the de-facto identity path), making tenant/workspace/user fully spoofable by any caller.
findings.evidence: middleware.rs:361-435 TenantContext::from_headers reads x-tenant-id/x-workspace-id/x-user-id; FromRequestParts Rejection = Infallible (always succeeds, no auth); grep TenantContext in handlers → 43 files

findings.fact: The only request-time API-key check is a non-constant-time String equality comparison against env-provided keys; no subtle/ConstantTime/ct_eq is used anywhere in the repo. The check is disabled unless EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY is set.
findings.evidence: middleware.rs:134  self.api_keys.iter().any(|k| k == key); server.rs:96-105 enables it only when EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY env is set (else AuthConfig::default() with enabled:false); grep constant_time|subtle|ct_eq → no matches

findings.fact: DB-backed API keys are created and Argon2-hashed into KV storage but are never validated against incoming requests — there is no extractor or middleware that looks up stored key_hash. Created API keys are thus non-functional for authentication. The create handler also hardcodes the owner as user_id = 'demo-user' instead of the authenticated user.
findings.evidence: handlers/auth/api_keys.rs:47  let user_id = "demo-user".to_string(); lines 56-73 hash+store key_hash; no request-time verify_password against key_hash anywhere in api/src (grep key_hash only hits creation, not validation)

findings.fact: Role parsing fails open: an unrecognized role string in a token silently becomes Role::User rather than being rejected.
findings.evidence: types.rs:28-30 Role::parse → s.parse().unwrap_or_default(); Role default = User (types.rs:20-21); used by Claims::role() at jwt.rs:132-134

findings.fact: An insecure decode-without-verification path exists (dangerous::insecure_decode) but is only defined, never called outside its own module — low risk currently.
findings.evidence: edgequake-auth/src/jwt.rs:226-230 decode_unverified uses dangerous::insecure_decode; grep shows no external call sites

findings.fact: ApiConfig (core) also models auth as disabled-by-default with empty plaintext api_keys, reinforcing that EdgeQuake ships auth-off by default.
findings.evidence: edgequake-core/src/config.rs:235-236  auth_enabled: false, api_keys: Vec::new()

open_questions: Is EdgeQuake intended to be reachable only on an internal Docker network (server.rs comment at line 86-95 implies so), or is its port ever exposed such that the hardcoded JWT secret + spoofable TenantContext headers become directly exploitable?

What component is responsible for setting X-Tenant-ID/X-Workspace-ID/X-User-ID — is there an upstream proxy (e.g., apps/web) that authenticates and injects these, and does it strip client-supplied copies to prevent spoofing?

Are the edgequake-auth login/JWT endpoints actually used by any client, or is the real auth fully delegated to the web app's better-auth/SayKnowWork layer with EdgeQuake JWT being effectively dead code?
Is there any plan to call AuthConfig::from_env() (so JWT_SECRET takes effect) and to wire the AuthUser/RequireAdmin extractors into routes, or is the simple env-key middleware the intended sole gate?

maps.area: EdgeQuake identity/tenant/workspace scope flow from inbound request to vector/query tenant filter (prompt.rs)
maps.summary: Tenant/workspace/user identity in EdgeQuake is carried entirely by three client-supplied HTTP headers: X-Tenant-ID, X-Workspace-ID, X-User-ID. TenantContext::from_headers reads them verbatim and its Axum extractor is infallible (never rejects). The only authentication layer is an optional shared static API key (api_key_auth), which is OFF unless EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY is set and, even when on, only gates access — it never binds the request to a tenant/workspace/user. A JwtService exists for /auth/login + /auth/me but the TenantContext extractor never consults it, so JWT claims do NOT drive scoping despite the routes.rs doc comment. Query handlers (execute_query, chat_completion, query_stream) take the header-derived workspace_id, look the workspace up in the DB, and use that workspace's tenant_id + the header workspace_id as the data scope passed into the engine; they verify the workspace exists but never verify the X-User-ID is a member of it. That scope flows via QueryRequest.params -> request.tenant_id()/workspace_id() -> matches_tenant_filter in prompt.rs, which (fail-closed) admits any record whose metadata.tenant_id and metadata.workspace_id string-equal the requested scope. Because the attacker supplies a matching scope, the fail-closed filter offers no protection against scope spoofing — it only stops leakage of untagged records.

files.role: TenantContext: extracts X-Tenant-ID/X-Workspace-ID/X-User-ID from headers (from_headers) and the infallible Axum extractor (FromRequestParts); also the only auth layer, api_key_auth (static shared key, off by default)
Auth wiring: api_key_auth enabled only if EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY env set; otherwise AuthConfig::default (disabled)
POST /api/v1/query handler: builds engine request scope from header-derived TenantContext + workspace lookup; no membership check
Chat completion handler: same header-derived scope; validates workspace EXISTS but not user membership; uses workspace.tenant_id as data scope
Streaming query handler: same header-derived scope pattern
QueryRequest: with_tenant_id/with_workspace_id store scope into params; tenant_id()/workspace_id() read it back
Engine entry: passes request.tenant_id()/workspace_id() into each mode-specific retrieval
Calls matches_tenant_filter / matches_tenant_filter_props on each retrieved record/edge
Calls matches_tenant_filter on each vector result
The fail-closed tenant filter: record must carry metadata.tenant_id + metadata.workspace_id (or props) string-equal to requested scope
Doc comment claims JWT-claims-first precedence for tenant context, which the code does not implement (misleading)

findings.fact: Tenant/workspace/user identity is read verbatim from client-supplied headers X-Tenant-ID, X-Workspace-ID, X-User-ID with zero validation.
findings.evidence: middleware.rs:377-398 TenantContext::from_headers: `headers.get("x-tenant-id")...`, `.get("x-workspace-id")`, `.get("x-user-id")` mapped straight to Option<String>

findings.fact: The TenantContext Axum extractor is infallible — it never rejects a request, so any/no header combination is accepted and flows downstream.
findings.evidence: middleware.rs:442-449 `type Rejection = std::convert::Infallible; ... Ok(TenantContext::from_headers(&parts.headers))`

findings.fact: There is no token that binds these headers to an authenticated identity. The only auth middleware is a single shared static API key check that does not derive or verify tenant/workspace/user.
findings.evidence: middleware.rs:166-215 api_key_auth only does `config.validate_api_key(&key)` against a static list; line 174 `if !config.enabled { return next.run(request).await }` skips entirely when disabled

findings.fact: API-key auth is OFF by default; it is enabled only if the EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY env var is set, and even then it is one shared key for all clients (not per-user).
findings.evidence: server.rs:96-105 `match std::env::var("EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY") { Ok(key) if !key.trim().is_empty() => ... AuthConfig::with_api_keys(...), _ => AuthConfig::default() }`; middleware.rs:103-105 default `enabled: false`

findings.fact: A JwtService exists (login/get_me verify_token) but the TenantContext extractor never consults it, so JWT claims do NOT populate the query scope despite the routes.rs documentation claiming JWT-claims-first precedence.
findings.evidence: routes.rs:79-82 comment 'extracted from: 1. JWT claims (tenant_id, workspace_id) 2. Headers...'; but middleware.rs:377-398 only reads headers; verify_token appears only in handlers/auth/session.rs:264-266, unrelated to scoping

findings.fact: In POST /api/v1/query the header-supplied workspace_id is used directly as the workspace scope, and the data tenant_id is resolved from that workspace's DB row — so supplying only a victim's X-Workspace-ID is enough; the attacker need not know the tenant_id. No check confirms the caller (X-User-ID) belongs to the workspace.
findings.evidence: query_execute.rs:87-104: `let workspace = ... get_workspace(&state, workspace_id)...; let data_tenant_id = workspace.map(|ws| ws.tenant_id.to_string()).or_else(|| tenant_ctx.tenant_id...); engine_request.with_tenant_id(data_tenant_id); ... engine_request.with_workspace_id(workspace_id.clone())`

findings.fact: chat_completion validates only that the workspace EXISTS (get_workspace), never that the user is a member; it then uses workspace.tenant_id as the data scope. Anonymous users with random UUIDs are auto-created, so X-User-ID is meaningless as identity.
findings.evidence: chat/completion.rs:99-113 workspace-exists validation; :181-188 `data_tenant_id = workspace.map(|ws| ws.tenant_id...).unwrap_or...; with_tenant_id(...); with_workspace_id(ws_id)`; :78 comment 'frontend generates random UUIDs for anonymous users' + INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING at :81-94

findings.evidence: query_stream.rs:36 `tenant_ctx: TenantContext`; :61-77 `let workspace = ... get_workspace(... workspace_id)...; engine_request.with_workspace_id(workspace_id.clone())`

findings.fact: No authorization/membership primitives exist anywhere in edgequake-api (no is_member/authorize/can_access). 'Unauthorized' is returned only when tenant/user headers are absent, never validated.
findings.evidence: grep across crates/edgequake-api/src found no is_member/membership/authorize/can_access; chat/completion.rs:54-63 returns ApiError::Unauthorized only via .ok_or(...) on missing headers

findings.fact: The scope reaches prompt.rs unchanged via QueryRequest.params: with_tenant_id/with_workspace_id store into params, tenant_id()/workspace_id() read them, and query_workspace passes them into every retrieval mode.
findings.evidence: engine.rs:215-244 params insert/read; query_workspace.rs:100-104 `request.tenant_id(), request.workspace_id()` passed to query_local_with_vector_storage etc.; query_modes.rs:54/70/132/181/240/367/415/549/582 and vector_queries.rs:37/69/85/226/265/432 call matches_tenant_filter[_props]

findings.fact: To pass the filter a record must carry, in its vector metadata JSON (or graph edge properties map), a `tenant_id` string field AND a `workspace_id` string field that string-equal the requested scope. The filter is fail-CLOSED (untagged records rejected), but the attacker simply supplies a matching scope so fail-closed gives no protection against spoofing.
findings.evidence: prompt.rs:24-36 `metadata.get("tenant_id").and_then(as_str) ... == tid else return false`, same for workspace_id; prompt.rs:54-65 props variant; prompt.rs:20-22 returns true when both scopes are None (unscoped queries see everything)

findings.fact: If a query is issued with no scope (no X-Tenant-ID/X-Workspace-ID headers), the filter short-circuits to allow ALL records regardless of tag — a global read of every tenant's data.
findings.evidence: prompt.rs:20-22 `if tenant_id.is_none() && workspace_id.is_none() { return true; }`

open_questions: Is the EdgeQuake API port actually network-isolated (Docker-internal only) in production, or reachable from the web tier / internet? The server.rs comment claims it is 'normally internal-only' — the severity of header spoofing depends on this. If the web app proxies user requests and forwards X-Workspace-ID from client-controlled state (localStorage), the spoof is reachable by end users.

maps.area: apps/web → EdgeQuake integration: base URL, auth headers, per-user identity, and PG re-filtering
maps.summary: The web app talks to the EdgeQuake Rust service through one thin client at apps/web/lib/edgequake/client.ts via raw fetch. Base URL comes from EDGEQUAKE_URL (default http://localhost:5403). On every request it sets Content-Type plus X-Workspace-ID and X-Tenant-ID (hard-coded default UUIDs from EDGEQUAKE_WORKSPACE_ID / EDGEQUAKE_TENANT_ID), adds X-User-ID only when a caller passes userId, and adds an Authorization: Bearer header only if EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY is non-empty (default empty, so by default NO auth header is sent). Identity (userId/tenantId/workspaceId) is stripped out of the JSON body and sent purely as headers; for indexing it is also duplicated into document metadata. Crucially, no caller ever passes tenantId or workspaceId, so every web user shares the SAME single EdgeQuake workspace/tenant — only X-User-ID varies, and EdgeQuake is documented to ignore X-User-ID for scoping (it is a single shared index). Real per-user/per-org isolation therefore happens entirely AFTER results return, by re-filtering EdgeQuake's document ids through PostgreSQL readableClause (directly, or via the filterVisibleSources/filterVisibleDocIds helpers in lib/edgequake/visibility.ts).

maps.area: EdgeQuake auth: how packages/mcp-server and apps/dashboard call EdgeQuake (vs the web app), and the per-user-JWT vs shared-key conflict
maps.summary: There are two distinct EdgeQuake callers besides the web app, with opposite auth models. (1) The MCP server has TWO outbound paths: its "direct EdgeQuake" tools (query, graph_*, workspace_*, document_*, health) talk to EdgeQuake via the edgequake-sdk client, forwarding the shared EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY plus a global tenant/workspace; its sayknowmind_* tools do NOT hit EdgeQuake at all — they proxy the SayKnowMind web app, forwarding the caller's per-user Bearer token. The direct tools are gated by rejectUserScopedEdgeQuakeTool(), which 403-blocks any request carrying per-user context (a user_mcp_keys key), so only the admin/shared key or stdio/anonymous callers reach EdgeQuake directly. (2) The dashboard talks to EdgeQuake directly and authenticates with a per-USER JWT (issued by EdgeQuake's own /api/v1/auth/login), sent as Authorization: Bearer <jwt> on every /api/v1/* call — it never sends a shared key. The conflict: EdgeQuake's optional api_key_auth middleware (enabled by setting EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY) validates the Bearer value by exact-string match against a static shared-key allowlist; a per-user JWT will never equal that key, so turning on shared-key enforcement would 401 the dashboard — both its login (login is not a public path) and all subsequent JWT-bearing data calls. This conflict is explicitly documented in a code comment in EdgeQuake's server.rs.

maps.area: EdgeQuake deployment topology & auth env-var plumbing (exposure + what "wiring auth" must not break)
maps.summary: EdgeQuake's RAG/graph HTTP API (port 8080, mapped to 5403 in native dev) is internal-only in every tracked deploy target: docker-compose declares no `ports:` for it (only web/dashboard/ai-server/mcp/relay are published), and the Helm chart gives it a ClusterIP Service with NO Ingress rule. The only auth EdgeQuake actually enforces is an optional shared-key check (`api_key_auth` middleware) that is OFF unless `EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY` is set in the EdgeQuake process env; the JWT/login/api-keys/tenant machinery referenced in routes/docs is unwired — no middleware verifies JWTs. In prod the real `.env` leaves `EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY` empty, so auth is disabled. Crucially, the EdgeQuake container itself is never handed `EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY` in either docker-compose or Helm, so the toggle is currently inert even if you set the secret. If shared-key auth were turned on, the web app would keep working (it forwards the key as `Authorization: Bearer`), but the MCP server (no key in compose or Helm) and the dashboard (sends a per-user JWT, not the shared key) would get 401s on every non-public route. JWT auth "by default" isn't a real option today — it would have to be built and wired first.

designs.canonical_identity:
EdgeQuake has two legitimate, opposite trust models and the design must keep both. The canonical identity is therefore PRINCIPAL-TYPED, resolved by a single combined auth layer:

(A) Trusted-service principal (web app, MCP server). Authenticates with the shared EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY. It has ALREADY authenticated the end user via better-auth and does the real isolation in Postgres readableClause (lib/visibility.ts, lib/edgequake/visibility.ts). For this principal EdgeQuake stays a single shared index and TRUSTS the X-Tenant-ID/X-Workspace-ID/X-User-ID headers verbatim — exactly today's behavior. This honors the memory directives 'don't revive EdgeQuake tenancy' and 'isolation is app-layer only'. EdgeQuake is NOT the isolation authority for the Open/web edition.

(B) End-user principal (dashboard). Authenticates with a per-user JWT issued by EdgeQuake /api/v1/auth/login. Here the canonical identity IS the JWT: subject claim `sub` = EdgeQuake user UUID (the principal), `role` = RBAC role, and `tenant_id`+`workspace_id` claims = the authorization scope. For this principal, identity is derived FROM verified claims, not trusted from spoofable headers.

Mapping to the existing prompt.rs filter: prompt.rs (matches_tenant_filter / matches_tenant_filter_props) does string equality on metadata.tenant_id and metadata.workspace_id. Those strings are what the JWT's tenant_id/workspace_id claims must equal. Today login() calls generate_token() which leaves both claims None (jwt.rs:88-89), so the JWT carries no scope and the dashboard is effectively unscoped. The canonical-identity fix is: at login, populate tenant_id (= the user's tenant UUID, the same value query_execute.rs already derives from workspace.tenant_id at line 94-97) and workspace_id (= the user's default/selected workspace) into the Claims, then have the combined auth layer STAMP the verified sub into X-User-ID (and, gated, tenant/workspace) before the request reaches the 43 TenantContext-based handlers. That way the existing TenantContext extractor and prompt.rs filter keep working unchanged, but for JWT callers their inputs are now verified rather than client-asserted. The single source of truth for both signing and verifying is AppState.jwt_service, which must be built from JWT_SECRET (see wiring).
designs.rationale:
Three independent defects compound today: (1) the JWT secret is the hardcoded 'change-me-in-production-256-bit-secret-key' because every AppState factory uses AuthConfig::default() and AuthConfig::from_env() is never called (config.rs:51, postgres.rs:293, memory.rs:46/182/272); (2) the only enforced layer is api_key_auth, which is a no-op unless EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY is set and only does a non-constant-time string == (middleware.rs:134, 173-176); (3) the dashboard sends a per-user JWT that api_key_auth can never match, so turning the shared key on 401s the dashboard's login, data calls, and WS — the conflict server.rs:92-95 already documents.

The security-first + zero-regression resolution is a single combined auth middleware that accepts EITHER the shared key (-> trusted-service principal, headers trusted as-is = current behavior) OR a valid JWT (-> end-user principal, identity from claims). This dissolves the shared-key-vs-JWT mismatch without forcing the dashboard onto the shared key (the option the existing comment proposes, which would break workspace switching and WS). It keeps the layer OPT-IN (only enforced when EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY or a new EDGEQUAKE_REQUIRE_AUTH is set), so the current Docker deploy — which ships EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY empty and the EdgeQuake port internal-only — is byte-for-byte unaffected until an operator opts in. The secret fix (route from_env into the factories + thread JWT_SECRET into the container) is independent of enforcement and safe to ship first, because from_env() still falls back to the dev default when JWT_SECRET is unset (no behavior change), but now a set JWT_SECRET actually takes effect.

from_env() strictness: if you hard-fail on the known-default secret, an operator who enables auth without setting JWT_SECRET will fail to start. Mitigation: only refuse when enforcement is ON; when enforcement is OFF keep the warn-and-fallback so non-auth deploys are untouched.

Stamping tenant/workspace from JWT claims could pin a dashboard user to their login-time workspace and break in-session workspace switching. Mitigation: always stamp X-User-ID from sub (anti-spoof, safe) but stamp tenant/workspace only when the header is absent, OR re-issue the JWT on workspace switch — a UX decision.
Constant-time compare swap is behavior-identical (same accept/reject), only removes the timing side-channel; no functional regression.

Default-on risk: keeping enforcement opt-in means a fresh deploy is still unauthenticated by default (same as today). The mitigation is the internal-only network posture (no published port in compose, ClusterIP + no Ingress in Helm); flag the move to default-on as a separate, later step once MCP/compose plumbing is verified.
designs.rollout: "Phased, opt-in first, to keep the current Docker deploy working untouched. Phase 0 (safe, ship immediately, no behavior change): fix the secret sourcing — config.rs from_env hardening + postgres.rs/memory.rs switch to from_env() + thread JWT_SECRET into the edgequake container (compose + Helm). With JWT_SECRET unset this is a no-op (falls back to dev default); with it set the real secret finally takes effect. Phase 1 (build, still inert by default): land the combined auth layer + constant-time compare + login claim population + api-keys owner fix. enforce stays false unless EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY or EDGEQUAKE_REQUIRE_AUTH is set, so default deploys are unchanged. Phase 2 (reconcile clients): ensure EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY reaches web, mcp-server (compose + Helm) and decide the /ws/* + /metrics whitelist; confirm dashboard JWT path end-to-end in a staging env. Phase 3 (opt-in enable): set JWT_SECRET (>=32 bytes) and EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY in one env change across all consumers; turn enforcement on in staging, validate web search, MCP tools, dashboard login/data/WS, then promote. Phase 4 (optional, later): flip to default-on (enforce unless explicitly disabled) once the plumbing is proven and DB-backed per-user API keys are wired. The canonical EC2 path (production-deploy.sh + host .env + main docker-compose.yml) is the deploy to validate; the CI deploy.yml path does not run EdgeQuake at all."

designs.canonical_identity:
Canonical identity at the EdgeQuake edge = the authenticated CALLER, proven by ONE of two credentials, not a re-derivation of per-user data scope:

1. Shared service key (EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY) — represents the trusted app tier (apps/web, packages/mcp-server). These clients already do per-user/per-org isolation downstream via Postgres readableClause re-filter (apps/web/lib/edgequake/visibility.ts), so EdgeQuake must NOT try to re-enforce that. Per the 'don't revive EdgeQuake tenancy' memory, the shared-key path stays trusted to assert X-Tenant-ID/X-Workspace-ID/X-User-ID and keeps the single-shared-workspace model.

2. Per-user JWT — for apps/dashboard, which treats EdgeQuake as genuinely multi-tenant. The JWT subject (`sub`) is the user UUID, plus `role`. Optional `tenant_id`/`workspace_id` claims (Claims already supports them at jwt.rs) carry scope. EdgeQuake issues this token at /api/v1/auth/login and can verify it because it holds the (now env-sourced) JWT_SECRET.

How it maps to prompt.rs filtering: today scope reaches prompt.rs::matches_tenant_filter via request.tenant_id()/workspace_id(), which come from the X-* headers (TenantContext). The fix makes the auth layer the AUTHORITY for those headers on the JWT path: when a JWT verifies, the middleware overwrites x-user-id (always, from `sub`) and, once login populates them, x-tenant-id/x-workspace-id (from claims) BEFORE handlers run. Because all 43 handlers read TenantContext from headers, this binds identity to the verified token with zero handler edits. On the shared-key path, headers pass through unchanged (web/mcp keep asserting scope; PG re-filter remains the isolation gate). This means the dashboard's existing JWT becomes a first-class credential and does NOT need to be rewritten to send the shared key.
designs.rationale:
Defect #2 is three coupled problems with very different blast radii, so I split them and only ship the low-risk parts default-on:

(1) Hardcoded JWT secret — cheapest, highest value. AuthConfig::from_env() exists but is never called; every AppState builds JwtService from AuthConfig::default() (postgres.rs:293, memory.rs:46/182/272), so JWT_SECRET is ignored. Switching those four call sites to from_env() makes the env var real. To honor 'fail-closed-when-configured', harden from_env() so that the known sentinel secret triggers a loud warning by default and a hard refusal-to-boot only when EDGEQUAKE_AUTH_STRICT=true. If JWT_SECRET is unset, behavior is byte-identical to today (same default secret) — zero blast radius.

(2) No auth attached — the api_key_auth layer is already on the router (commit ff03128) but inert because EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY is empty AND the edgequake container is never even handed the var (docker-compose.yml:60-68, helm edgequake.yaml). I keep it OPT-IN, but (a) make the toggle actually reachable by threading the var into the edgequake + mcp containers, and (b) teach the gate to accept a verified JWT in addition to the shared key, so flipping it on does not 401 the dashboard. Default OFF = zero blast radius; this is the migration path, not default-on enforcement.

(3) Spoofable identity headers — biggest blast radius (43 handlers + the web app's deliberate header-trust model). I do the one safe sub-step now: when a JWT verifies, overwrite x-user-id from `sub` so identity is bound to the token without touching handlers. Full scope-binding (populate tenant/workspace claims at login + membership authorization + strip client headers) is staged as phase 2, because EdgeQuake is internal-only (no published ports; ClusterIP, no Ingress) and the web path's real isolation is the PG re-filter — so the live exploitability is gated by the network today.

This sequence closes the secret defect immediately and default-on, makes enforcement a one-flag operation that won't break any of the four clients, and leaves a clear path to header-binding — all without a big-bang.

# Adversarial Critique: EdgeQuake Auth Wiring (Design A vs B)

## 1. Verdict per design

### Design A (security-first) — strong, but over-reaches and has one hard correctness gap
**Correct against MAP:** dual-principal model; combined layer accepting shared-key OR JWT; routing `postgres.rs:293` + `memory.rs` factories to `from_env()`; threading `JWT_SECRET`/`EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY` into the edgequake + mcp containers (compose + Helm); constant-time compare; the observation that the documented `server.rs:92-95` breakage is dissolved by accepting JWTs rather than forcing the dashboard onto the shared key. All verified consistent with MAP.

**Gaps / defects:**
- **HARD GAP — public_paths for `/auth/login` never added.** A's combined-layer step relies on `is_public_path` but never updates the list. MAP is explicit: `/api/v1/auth/login` is NOT public (`middleware.rs:107-113`), carries no token, so under `enforce=true` A's layer 401s login itself — the exact failure MAP calls out. A's only public-paths edit (routes.rs step) discusses `/metrics` and `/ws/*`, not login/refresh. This must be fixed or enforcement is unusable. **Design B catches this** (its Step 4 adds `/auth/login`,`/auth/refresh`).
- **Over-reach: claim-based tenant/workspace stamping in the same pass.** A's login step says "look up the user's tenant … reuse the same tenant `query_execute.rs:94` derives." That's incorrect: `query_execute` derives `tenant_id` from a **workspace row that came from a header**, not from the user. I verified `session.rs` login only does `generate_token(user_uuid, user.role)` — there is **no user→workspace/tenant membership source in the login path at all.** So "populate tenant_id/workspace_id at login" is not a safe autonomous edit; it depends on a membership/default-workspace lookup that does not exist yet. A treats this as in-scope phase-1 work; it is actually a blocked design decision.
- **`EDGEQUAKE_REQUIRE_AUTH` (JWT-only enforcement) is net-new surface** with no consumer that needs it confirmed (dashboard deployment status is an open question). Adds a second toggle and a "refuse-to-boot on default secret" hard-fail path. Reasonable but speculative; defer.

### Design B (minimal) — better sequencing and blast-radius discipline, slightly under-specified on hardening
**Correct against MAP:** identical dual-principal conclusion; same `from_env()` routing; **explicitly adds `/auth/login`+`/auth/refresh` to public_paths** (the thing A misses); extends existing `AuthState` with `Option<Arc<JwtService>>` rather than inventing a parallel state struct (smaller diff, lower regression risk); correctly sequences scope-claim population + membership authorization into an explicit Phase 2/3 *after* confirming exploitability is network-gated. B's framing ("split #2 into three problems with different blast radii") is the more honest read of the MAP.

**Gaps / defects:**
- B switches **all** `memory.rs` factories (46/182/272) to `from_env()` including what is likely `test_state`. MAP doesn't label which is the test factory. **A's caution is correct here** — keep the test factory on `AuthConfig::default()` for deterministic tests, or you risk env-dependent test flakiness.
- B leaves `EDGEQUAKE_AUTH_STRICT` semantics loose (warn-vs-panic) and doesn't address `/ws/*` + `/metrics` until "before default-on" — acceptable for opt-in but should be named as a blocker before any enable.
- B's Phase-2 note also assumes login can populate tenant/workspace claims without confronting the missing membership source (same flaw as A, but B at least quarantines it to a later phase).

**Bottom line:** B's *phasing and minimalism* are superior and lower-risk; A's *combined-layer construction detail* (principal extension, identity stamping, constant-time) is more complete. The synthesized plan takes B's spine and A's flesh.

## 2. Claims NOT supported by (or contradicted by) the MAP

- **A & B — login can source the user's tenant/workspace.** Unsupported and effectively contradicted. Verified: `session.rs` login uses only `user.role`; no user→workspace/tenant mapping exists. The tenant in the query path comes from a header-supplied workspace, not the user. **This is the single biggest hand-wave in both designs.**
- **A — "mirror the claim copy already done in jwt.rs refresh_token (lines 242-243)."** Misstated but harmless: `refresh_token(&self, claims: &Claims)` (jwt.rs:236) re-signs the *passed* claims, so scope is preserved automatically if the original token carried it — there is nothing to "mirror." No code change needed there.
- **A — data-scope alignment is silently assumed.** Neither design notes that web-app-indexed vectors are tagged with the web app's **hardcoded** `EDGEQUAKE_TENANT_ID(...0002)/WORKSPACE_ID(...0003)` (client.ts), while a dashboard JWT would carry *different* tenant/workspace UUIDs. `prompt.rs` does string-equality on those tags. So stamping dashboard claims as scope could match **zero** documents. Unsupported assumption that JWT-claim scope and indexed metadata share a namespace. Real efficacy risk.
- **Confirmed-true claims I checked (not defects):** `with_tenant_id`/`with_workspace_id` Claims builders exist (jwt.rs:107/113); `generate_token_with_claims` exists (jwt.rs:186); `sha2 = "0.10"` is present in edgequake-api Cargo.toml (line 58). `subtle` is NOT currently a dep — adding it (A) is fine, or reuse sha2 to hash-then-compare.
- **B — "tokens are short-lived (24h)."** Not in MAP; token expiry duration is unverified. Don't rely on it in deploy comms.

## 3. Canonical identity — recommendation

**Adopt the principal-typed dual model both designs converge on.** It is correct and honors the memory directives ("don't revive EdgeQuake tenancy", "isolation is app-layer only"):

- **Trusted-service principal** (web, mcp): shared `EDGEQUAKE_API_KEY`. Headers `X-Tenant/Workspace/User-ID` pass through **verbatim, unchanged**. Postgres `readableClause` remains the *sole* isolation authority for the Open/web edition. EdgeQuake stays a single shared index.
- **End-user principal** (dashboard): per-user JWT; `sub` is canonical caller identity.

**But split the identity decision in two, against both designs' instinct to do it all at once:**

1. **Safe now (autonomous):** on a verified JWT, **overwrite `X-User-ID` from `sub` only.** `sub` is always present, this is pure anti-spoof, and it touches zero handlers (the 43 `TenantContext` readers keep working).
2. **Blocked / human-decision (do NOT do in the first pass):** stamping `X-Tenant-ID`/`X-Workspace-ID` from JWT claims. This requires (a) a user→default-workspace/tenant membership source that **does not exist** in the login path today, and (b) confirmation that dashboard tenant/workspace UUIDs actually align with how vectors are tagged at index time (they currently do not — web indexes under hardcoded UUIDs). Until both are resolved, claim-based scope stamping would either match nothing or silently broaden scope.

So: **caller-authentication first; scope-binding is a separate, later, design-gated phase.** EdgeQuake authenticates *who is calling*; it does not become the per-user data-isolation authority for the web path.
